content.section_title: Acute heart failure (HF) complicating acute coronary syndrome (ACS)
content.summary: Patients with ACS complicated by acute HF require urgent, coordinated management of both conditions following current ESC HF recommendations. Consider diuretics, vasodilators, inotropic agents, vasopressors, and selected mechanical circulatory support; invasive respiratory support and/or renal replacement therapy may be required in some cases.
recommendations: Follow current ESC Guidelines on HF and ancillary documents for management of acute HF.
Consider diuretics, vasodilators, inotropic agents, and vasopressors per established algorithms.
Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) may be considered in selected cases.
Invasive respiratory support and/or renal replacement therapy may be required where indicated.
diagnostic_and_interventional_management: Patients with acute HF (including those with cardiogenic shock) complicating ACS require immediate invasive coronary angiography (ICA) when indicated.
Emergency echocardiography/chest ultrasonography should be performed to assess LV and RV function, regional wall motion abnormalities, valvular function, and possible mechanical complications.
Transfer to a PCI centre for immediate coronary angiography and PCI of the infarct-related artery (IRA) if needed; emergency CABG if coronary anatomy unsuitable for PCI.

mechanical_circulatory_support_evidence.overall_statement: The clinical benefit of percutaneous MCS devices and/or VA-ECMO in ACS is unclear.
key_points: Micro-axial MCS devices have not been shown to reduce 30-day mortality compared with IABP in observational studies.
A large retrospective registry (>48,000 patients, >80% ACS) found micro-axial MCS support associated with higher mortality and bleeding rates compared with IABP.
Propensity-matched analyses confined to patients with cardiogenic shock also associated micro-axial MCS with more complications and higher mortality than IABP.
IABP-SHOCK II trial: routine use of IABP in patients with ACS and cardiogenic shock did not reduce 30-day, 1-year, or 6-year mortality.
No demonstrated benefit of LVAD in patients with ACS; observational data suggest possible harm, so caution is advised until further RCT evidence is available.

mechanical_complications.statement: Mechanical complications may occur in the first days following MI, most commonly in patients presenting with STEMI.
mechanical_complications.note: Mechanical complications are life-threatening and require prompt identification and management.
